name: A2 organic applied drawing/data practice and concise memory gaps
scope: A-level only, full revision scope; no November mock eligibility assumed

cards.front: Give one typical use of Terylene polyester.
cards.back: Textile fibres, such as clothing fabric.

cards.front: Give one typical use of nylon 6,6.
Give one typical use of Kevlar.
cards.back: Protective fabrics or high-strength reinforcing fibres.

cards.front: Which groups form hydrogen bonds between typical polyamide chains?
cards.back: N–H groups donate to carbonyl oxygen atoms on other chains.

cards.front: What functional group forms when a nitrile group is reduced?
What group replaces a nitro group on an aromatic ring upon reduction?
cards.back: An amino group, –NH₂, giving an aromatic amine.

questions.prompt: On paper, draw both three-dimensional enantiomers of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, using solid and hashed wedges at the chiral carbon. Explain why your two drawings are enantiomers and predict how equal concentrations affect plane-polarised light.
markPoints: Carbon 2 is correctly identified as attached to CH₃, CH₂CH₃, H and OH.
Both drawings show a tetrahedral carbon with a clear three-dimensional wedge-and-dash representation.
All four attached groups retain the correct connectivity in each drawing.
The arrangement at the chiral carbon is inverted between the drawings, not merely rotated on the paper.
The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images.
Pure enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in magnitude but in opposite directions under identical conditions.

questions.prompt: A model glycerol triester contains one ethanoate, one propanoate and one butanoate residue, each attached to a different oxygen of glycerol. On paper, draw its complete condensed or displayed structure. Identify the linkages and predict the molecular products of complete hydrolysis. Do not give a laboratory method.
markPoints: The glycerol framework is correctly shown as CH₂–CH–CH₂ with an oxygen substituent on each carbon.
One oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₃ (ethanoate residue).
A second oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₃ (propanoate residue).
The third oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butanoate residue).
All three –O–C(=O)– units are correctly recognised as ester links.
Complete acid hydrolysis yields one glycerol molecule and one molecule each of ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid.

questions.prompt: A reference pure organic solid has a melting point of 122.4 °C. Sample A melts over 116.5–120.0 °C; sample B melts over 121.8–122.4 °C. Assess which sample is likely purer and what the data can and cannot prove.
markPoints: Sample B is more consistent with a pure sample than A.
Sample B has a narrower melting range of 0.6 °C.
Sample A has a broader melting range of 3.5 °C.
An impurity generally lowers and broadens the observed melting range of a solid.
The melting data alone do not establish the compound's identity or absolute purity conclusively.

questions.prompt: Hydrogenation of cyclohexene releases 120 kJ mol⁻¹. A hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds would therefore release three times this amount. The measured enthalpy change for hydrogenation of benzene is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the theoretical value and the extra stabilisation of benzene, and explain what it implies about bonding and substitution.
markPoints: The theoretical value for three isolated C=C bonds is 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
The measured benzene hydrogenation enthalpy is less exothermic than −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
The stabilisation difference is 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹.
The π electrons in benzene are delocalised over the ring.
Delocalisation lowers the energy of benzene relative to the hypothetical three-isolated-bond structure.
Substitution is favoured over addition because it preserves the delocalised aromatic system.

questions.prompt: On paper, draw a polyester repeating unit formed from propane-1,3-diol, HO–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–OH, and butanedioic acid, HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH. Use square brackets and continuation bonds. Explain the type of polymerisation and show the linkage that repeats.
markPoints: The three-carbon diol segment –O–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–O– appears in the repeat unit.
The diacid segment –C(=O)–CH₂–CH₂–C(=O)– appears in the repeat unit.
The oxygen of each alcohol-derived end connects to an acid-derived carbonyl carbon, forming ester links.
The repeating unit is correctly bracketed with bonds extending through the bracket edges.
The link is identified as –C(=O)–O– (or –O–C(=O)–).
This is condensation polymerisation with elimination of a small molecule such as water when bonds form.

questions.prompt: A polyamide has the repeating unit [–NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–C(=O)–(CH₂)₂–C(=O)–]ₙ. On paper, draw the two monomers from which it was formed. Name the bond type between monomer fragments and explain the intermolecular attractions between typical polyamide chains.
markPoints: The diamine monomer is H₂N–(CH₂)₄–NH₂.
The second monomer is HOOC–(CH₂)₂–COOH.
The repeating structure includes the amide linkage –C(=O)–NH–.
The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from N–H groups on adjacent polyamide chains.
Hydrogen bonding gives an intermolecular attraction between typical polyamide chains.
Amide linkages can undergo hydrolysis, unlike the all-carbon backbone of a typical polyalkene.

questions.prompt: For alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, draw the predominant simple structural forms in acidic solution, as a zwitterion, and in alkaline solution. Label the overall charge on each. Use the protonation states rather than a practical method.
markPoints: The acidic form is CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COOH.
The acidic form has overall charge +1.
The zwitterion is CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COO⁻.
The zwitterion has overall charge zero despite internal positive and negative charges.
The alkaline form is CH₃CH(NH₂)COO⁻.
The alkaline form has overall charge −1.

questions.prompt: Draw the full condensed structural formula of the tripeptide Ala–Gly–Ser (alanine–glycine–serine) with a free N terminus on the alanine end. Use side chains –CH₃ for alanine, –H for glycine and –CH₂OH for serine. Label the peptide links, and describe what complete hydrolysis yields.
markPoints: The N terminus is H₂N–CH(CH₃)–C(=O)– for alanine.
The central glycine residue is –NH–CH₂–C(=O)–.
The final serine residue is –NH–CH(CH₂OH)–COOH.
Two correctly placed –C(=O)–NH– peptide linkages join the three residues.
The tripeptide has one free N terminus and one free carboxyl terminus.
Complete hydrolysis of the peptide bonds yields alanine, glycine and serine.

questions.prompt: Three labelled drawings represent a protein: A shows just the ordered amino-acid sequence; B shows a section coiled into an α-helix with dotted links between backbone groups; C shows the whole chain folded, with a labelled sulfur–sulfur bridge between side chains. On paper, sketch and annotate one of the two higher-order structures. Identify the level shown by A, B and C and explain the bonding features.
markPoints: A represents primary structure: the amino-acid sequence.
B represents secondary structure, specifically an α-helix.
The dotted links in B represent hydrogen bonds between backbone groups.
C represents tertiary structure, the overall three-dimensional folding of the chain.
The sulfur–sulfur bridge in C is a covalent disulfide bond involving sulfur-containing side chains.
The student's annotated sketch correctly represents an α-helix with hydrogen bonding or an overall folded chain with a disulfide bridge.

questions.prompt: A fictional enzyme has an asymmetric active site with three binding regions. Enantiomer P positions all three matching groups towards these regions; its mirror image Q can align only two groups at once. Explain why the enzyme can discriminate between P and Q, and why this need not imply a difference in their molecular formulae.
markPoints: P and Q are enantiomers with the same molecular formula and connectivity.
They have different three-dimensional arrangements and are non-superimposable mirror images.
The enzyme's active site has a specific three-dimensional shape and binding-group arrangement.
P can position all three complementary groups for favourable binding.
Q cannot necessarily achieve the same three-point alignment, so it may bind more weakly or not react.
This is stereospecificity; it depends on spatial fit and interactions, not simply chemical composition.

questions.prompt: A compound has formula C₃H₆O₂. Its ¹³C NMR spectrum has three environments, with shifts near δ 20, 52 and 171 ppm. Its ¹H spectrum has just two singlets, each integrating to 3 H, near δ 2.1 and 3.7 ppm. Distinguish methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃) from propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), using all the data.
markPoints: The molecular formula is consistent with either of the stated structural isomers.
Three ¹³C environments are consistent with the three non-equivalent carbon atoms in methyl ethanoate.
The carbon near δ 171 ppm is consistent with a carbonyl environment.
The two ¹H integrations of 3:3 show two distinct three-proton environments.
Two singlets fit methyl ethanoate's CH₃CO– and –OCH₃ groups, without neighbouring non-equivalent hydrogens on adjacent carbon atoms.
Propanoic acid would give a CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet in the simple first-order model, not two three-proton singlets.
The supported structure is methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃.

questions.subtopic: Interpret a complete TLC mixture and standards
questions.prompt: A TLC plate developed in one solvent has a solvent front 8.0 cm above the baseline. Pure standards A, B and C have spots 2.0, 4.0 and 6.0 cm above the baseline respectively. An unknown U has two spots at 2.0 and 6.0 cm. Calculate the two Rf values for U, suggest its components and explain a limitation of this identification.
markPoints: The Rf formula is distance travelled by a spot divided by solvent-front distance.
The lower U spot has Rf = 2.0/8.0 = 0.25.
The upper U spot has Rf = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75.
Under the same conditions, U's lower spot matches standard A.
Under the same conditions, U's upper spot matches standard C, with no spot matching B.
Matching Rf values are suggestive rather than conclusive proof of chemical identity; another solvent or analysis could provide confirmation.

questions.prompt: A gas chromatogram recorded under fixed conditions has standards A, B and C with retention times 2.40, 5.20 and 7.90 minutes. An unknown has two peaks at 2.42 and 5.18 minutes. State the likely components, whether C is evidenced, and why a GC–MS measurement could improve confidence.
markPoints: The peak near 2.42 min is consistent with standard A at 2.40 min.
The peak near 5.18 min is consistent with standard B at 5.20 min.
No peak close to C's 7.90-minute retention time is shown.
Identification by retention time must use comparable chromatographic conditions.
Retention time alone is not definitive because different substances may co-elute.
GC–MS gives mass-spectral information on the separated components and can help support an identity.

questions.subtopic: Recognise amine and ammonium structural classes
questions.prompt: On paper, draw the displayed or condensed formulae of methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine and the tetramethylammonium cation. Label each as primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary. Explain how the nitrogen lone pair differs in the cation.
markPoints: CH₃NH₂ is a primary amine with one carbon-containing substituent on nitrogen.
(CH₃)₂NH is a secondary amine with two carbon-containing substituents.
(CH₃)₃N is a tertiary amine with three carbon-containing substituents.
(CH₃)₄N⁺ is a quaternary ammonium cation with four carbon-containing substituents.
The quaternary ammonium nitrogen has a formal positive charge.
The quaternary ammonium ion has no available nitrogen lone pair, unlike the neutral amines.
